name: authenticator
intent: Verify the identity a subject claims from mechanism-specific credentials and return one normalized principal or an explicit failure, so callers can select or replace password, certificate, token, Kerberos or passkey verification without coupling login, session, audit or authorization code to a credential format.
problem: A request must decide whether presented evidence proves a subject's identity, but password, client-certificate, OIDC/JWT, Kerberos and passkey checks differ by deployment, tenant and channel. If one mechanism is hard-wired into the request path, every caller learns its credential format; adding OIDC, migrating from LDAP or accepting service tokens becomes a cross-cutting change, while comparison, retry/lockout and verifier-failure handling drift between endpoints.
context: Systems that verify identities at a trust boundary - HTTP APIs, message endpoints, CLIs or device onboarding - where more than one credential form is in use or expected, the mechanism is selectable per deployment, tenant or route, and downstream authorization, session and audit code needs a mechanism-independent principal. It is also the seam for composing MFA or step-up checks and for replacing an external identity provider in tests.
benefits: New mechanisms arrive as new implementations behind one interface: adding OIDC, mutual TLS or passkeys does not touch call sites, session code or authorization rules.
Callers receive one normalized principal type instead of credential-shaped objects, so authorization, audit and session code never parse a credential format.
Testability: a fake authenticator (always-allow, always-deny, fixed principal) replaces the corporate identity provider in tests while the real gate stays in the exercised path.

Security policy has a single home: retry and lockout limits, algorithm allow-lists, clock-skew checks, constant-time comparison, auditing and credential hygiene live in the authenticator instead of being scattered across endpoints.
Deployment flexibility: the mechanism set and its order are configuration (scheme names, backend lists, per-tenant settings), so one build serves password-only sites and federated sites.
Composition: primary and additional authenticators chain with explicit semantics (required, sufficient, optional), which is how multi-factor and step-up authentication are expressed declaratively.
tradeoffs: Indirection and traceability: an inline credential check is one stack frame; a configured mechanism adds registry lookup, dynamic dispatch and often a remote call, so debugging starts with determining which authenticator actually ran.

Lowest-common-denominator interface: normalizing everything to a username/password-shaped credential hides mechanism-specific evidence (certificate channel binding, passkey attestation, token scopes) unless the abstraction is explicitly allowed to carry it.
Single point of failure: one misordered chain, expired client secret or unreachable identity provider now fails uniformly for every caller, because all of them depend on the same seam.

Mechanism confusion and downgrade: several registered authenticators that accept overlapping credential shapes let an attacker pick the weakest, and fallback chains that treat verification failure as anonymous turn the pattern into a bypass.

The security effort shifts rather than disappears: the pattern centralizes where verification happens, not how - comparison bugs, token validation and secret handling remain the implementer's responsibility and are now reachable from every call site.
Per-request cost: external verification (directory bind, token introspection, certificate revocation lookup) on every request unless sessions or caching sit above the authenticator.

participants.responsibility: Declares the single authentication operation over an abstract credential and hides which mechanism verifies it; the only face callers, sessions and tests depend on.

Implements verification for one credential technology - password, certificate, bearer/OIDC token, Kerberos ticket, passkey assertion - consulting its identity store and returning a principal or a failure.
The evidence presented by the subject (password, certificate, assertion, token). Its format belongs to the mechanism, never to the caller.
The verified identity: the normalized, mechanism-independent output that authorization, sessions and audit consume.
Maps configured mechanism names (schemes) and selection policy (chain order, required/sufficient/optional) onto the concrete authenticator instances.
Presents credentials on behalf of the subject - over HTTP headers, a TLS handshake, a message or a device gesture - and receives the challenge or failure response when verification fails.

use_cases: A web application that must accept password login, federated OIDC login and API bearer tokens, all producing the same session principal.
An enterprise service deployed at sites with different directories (LDAP/AD, Kerberos, local database) that selects its mechanism per deployment without a code fork.
A microservice that validates self-issued JWTs for normal traffic and falls back to token introspection at the corporate authorization server for opaque tokens.
A CLI or desktop agent with pluggable credential providers: OS keychain, smart card, TPM-backed passkey or an interactive password prompt.
Step-up authentication: a second authenticator (one-time code, WebAuthn assertion) chained behind the primary one for sensitive operations.
Test and simulation environments where a fake authenticator replaces the identity provider while the production authentication gate remains the exercised path.

A passkey Relying Party (RP) backend that implements WebAuthn registration and authentication ceremonies: generates session-bound challenges (CSPRNG, 16+ bytes, 60-120s TTL), verifies authenticator assertions (origin, challenge replay prevention via single-use challenge, UP/UV flags, signCount monotonicity, signature), and issues a normalized session principal.

Zero-trust microservice mesh: SPIFFE/SPIRE-issued short-lived X.509 SVIDs via mTLS, where each service presents a workload certificate encoded with its SPIFFE ID; the authenticator verifies the certificate chain and extracts the cryptographic workload identity as the principal.

Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) token storage: the BFF holds access/refresh tokens in server-side memory or encrypted httpOnly cookies, issuing scoped session cookies to the SPA; the authenticator seam is the BFF's token refresh logic, not the browser.

OAuth2 authorization code + PKCE public client: the authenticator validates the code, verifier and state on the backend, rotates refresh tokens on every use, and issues short-lived JWTs; the same interface normalizes this flow alongside password and passkey flows.

A Java service can keep application code independent of the mechanism by driving configured JAAS LoginModules through LoginContext, while Spring Security exposes the same seam through AuthenticationProvider and ProviderManager.
A Keycloak deployment can add a custom credential or challenge step by implementing the Authenticator and AuthenticatorFactory SPIs and placing that execution in an authentication flow.

A Node.js service can install Passport.js strategies such as passport-local or passport-openidconnect, register them with passport.use(), and normalize the verify callback's user into the application's principal.

A Django project extends authentication beyond its user database by listing custom backends in AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS; django.contrib.auth.authenticate() tries each backend's authenticate(request, **credentials) in order, first success wins, and the returned User is the normalized principal.

An ASP.NET Core app registers one named scheme per mechanism (AddJwtBearer, AddCookie, a custom AuthenticationHandler) and composes them with policy schemes (AddPolicyScheme, ForwardDefaultSelector) so one endpoint routes bearer and cookie requests to the right handler without branching in the controller.

The Kubernetes API server authenticates every request through a union of authenticators - front-proxy request-header (X-Remote-User / X-Remote-Group, trusted only after the proxy's client certificate validates against the configured CA), X.509 client certificates and TokenReview webhooks with cached decisions - and hands the resulting normalized user info to authorization.
avoid_when: Exactly one fixed mechanism exists and will never change: a direct check against the user record is simpler and clearer than an interface.

The framework already owns the seam - configure its provider instead of writing your own authenticator (Spring Security, ASP.NET Core authentication schemes, Django authentication backends, Ktor Authentication, Vapor Authenticator, Warden strategies).
Authentication is terminated outside the application (identity-aware proxy, service-mesh mTLS, API gateway with its own authentication); no mechanism choice is left inside.
One-off scripts and prototypes: OS or language facilities plus a direct comparison are enough, and the interface is noise.
The decision is really authorization (what may this principal do) rather than identity proof; use authorization-enforcer or a policy/guard after authentication instead of widening the authenticator.
A request gate only needs to require an already established identity: use authentication-enforcer for enforcement, and keep credential verification in the authenticator.
The task is to carry or persist an already verified identity between handlers or requests: use security-context or secure-session-manager, not another authenticator.
anti_patterns: An if/else-if ladder over mechanism names inside the login handler -> every new scheme edits the handler and duplicates comparison and failure mapping -> resolve a configured authenticator from a registry instead.

A leaky abstraction that returns mechanism-specific claims or principal types -> downstream code branches on the credential format -> normalize to one principal and carry richer evidence as optional detail.

Negative authentication that treats verification failure as anonymous or swallows verifier errors -> an unverified request continues as if it had passed -> fail closed and distinguish invalid credentials from provider unavailability.

Authorization smuggled into the authenticator through permission checks or tenant filtering -> identity proof becomes coupled to changing policy and can grant unintended access -> let authorization-enforcer or policy guards decide after authentication.

Home-made credential verification with non-constant-time comparison, hand-parsed tokens or custom cryptography -> edge cases and cryptographic mistakes turn into account takeover -> use a maintained protocol/KDF library and validate its complete contract.
Storing bearer tokens in localStorage or sessionStorage -> any XSS can exfiltrate a reusable token -> keep tokens server-side or in protected httpOnly cookies with the required CSRF controls.

Accepting a JWT without an explicit algorithm allowlist and issuer, audience and expiry checks -> an alg:none or wrong-issuer token is treated as an identity -> verify the signature against the intended key and validate every registered claim.
Skipping WebAuthn user-verification enforcement -> an assertion with UV=0 passes when a PIN or biometric was required -> reject it unless the requested userVerification policy is satisfied.
design_principles: Program to an interface, not an implementation: callers depend on the authentication operation and the principal type, never on a mechanism.
Single responsibility: verify identity (Authenticator), decide what the identity may do (policy/guard), and keep it between requests (session manager) are separate concerns.
Open/closed principle: new mechanisms are added as implementations plus configuration, without modifying call sites.
Information hiding: credential formats and identity-store details stay inside the mechanism; callers see only the principal.
Fail closed and deny by default: an unavailable or inconclusive authenticator must not yield access, and complete mediation means every request passes the same gate.
best_practices: Normalize the output to one principal type and attach mechanism-specific detail as optional, ignorable attributes.
Name mechanisms in configuration (scheme or backend lists) and resolve them per route or tenant; keep mechanism branching out of handlers.
Distinguish invalid credentials from verification unavailability in results, metrics and logs, and fail closed for both.
Constrain each mechanism to the credential it can verify, and define chain semantics explicitly (first match, required, sufficient) to prevent downgrade.
Keep authenticators stateless per request; hold cross-request identity in the session manager, and never log credentials or secrets.
Rate-limit and lock out per subject and per source, and audit every attempt together with the mechanism that handled it.

For WebAuthn/passkey: generate challenges with a CSPRNG (minimum 16 bytes), store them server-side with a 60-120s TTL, enforce single-use by deleting after verification or expiry, and always verify the UP (User Present) flag and the UV (User Verified) flag when userVerification is required.
For WebAuthn/passkey: enforce signCount monotonicity for device-bound credentials (BE=0) to detect cloning; skip monotonicity checks for synced passkeys (BE=1) which may report signCount=0.
For WebAuthn/passkey: verify the origin in clientDataJSON against an explicit allowlist using exact string equality; do not use regex or suffix matching which enables subdomain-phishing bypass.
For OAuth2/OIDC: use Authorization Code + PKCE for all public clients (SPAs, mobile apps); the implicit flow is deprecated (RFC 9700) and must not be used.

For OAuth2/OIDC: rotate refresh tokens on every use; store only the hash (e.g., HMAC-SHA256) of the refresh token in the database; on reuse detection, revoke the entire token family and force re-authentication.

For JWT validation: always verify signature (against JWKS key matched by kid), iss, aud, exp; use an explicit algorithm allowlist (never accept alg:none); never trust a decoded payload without signature verification.
For JWT access tokens: keep lifetimes short (5-15 minutes) to limit the revocation window; pair with refresh token rotation for sessions that outlast a single access token.

For token storage: store access tokens in server-side memory or httpOnly cookies; never in localStorage or sessionStorage (XSS-readable); refresh tokens belong in server-side storage or encrypted httpOnly cookies with CSRF protection.

For service-to-service: prefer short-lived, auto-rotated workload certificates (SPIFFE/SPIRE X.509 SVIDs) over long-lived API keys or static secrets; mTLS combined with SPIFFE ID-based authorization enforces identity at the transport layer.

For DPoP (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession, RFC 9449): bind access tokens to the client's key pair via the cnf claim and require a DPoP proof JWT on every request; this prevents stolen tokens from being usable without the private key.

related_patterns_notes.authentication-enforcer: requires a previously established authenticated identity at a request boundary; Authenticator performs credential verification and creates that identity.
related_patterns_notes.subject-descriptor: describes a subject's attributes or claims; Authenticator verifies evidence for that subject.
related_patterns_notes.security-context: stores and propagates a verified principal; Authenticator is the component that verifies the presented credential.
related_patterns_notes.secure-session-manager: persists authenticated state across requests; Authenticator establishes the identity that may be persisted.
related_patterns_notes.authorization-enforcer: decides whether an authenticated principal may perform an action; Authenticator only establishes who the principal is.
related_patterns_notes.strategy: supplies interchangeable behavior for any algorithm; Authenticator is the identity-verification specialization of that idea.
related_patterns_notes.adapter: translates one interface into another; Authenticator may adapt a provider but still owns the trust decision.
related_patterns_notes.spiffe-workload-identity: issues or names workload credentials; Authenticator verifies the SVID and extracts the workload principal.
related_patterns_notes.dpop-token-binding: binds a token to a proof-of-possession key; Authenticator verifies that proof but does not replace authorization.
related_patterns_notes.paseto: defines a secure token format; it is credential material that an Authenticator must validate, not an authentication policy.
related_patterns_notes.opa-authorization: evaluates policy for an already identified subject; it must not be used to prove possession of credentials.
